answer: The proposed mechanisms by which GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce cardiovascular events include mediation through both glycemic and non-glycemic pathways. Causal mediation analyses of the LEADER and SUSTAIN-6 trials identified HbA1c, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and systolic blood pressure (SBP) as significant mediators of the treatment effect on three-point major adverse cardiovascular events (3P-MACE) [3][10]. Beyond these traditional risk factors, GLP-1RAs are proposed to protect against atherosclerosis by reducing vascular and systemic inflammation independently of changes in cholesterol, blood glucose, and body weight [5], with preclinical evidence of reduced expression of TNF, MCP-1, and IL-6 in macrophages [7]. Additional proposed mechanisms include improved endothelial function via enhanced nitric oxide bioavailability and eNOS activation, blood pressure reduction through natriuresis and reduced sympathetic activity, and anti-thrombotic effects [4][8]. However, the precise mechanism remains unclear, and inter-organ communication, possibly via neural pathways, may contribute to GLP-1RA-mediated cardiovascular protection [7].

A large real-world propensity-matched cohort found that GLP-1 RA use was associated with a small increased risk of acute pancreatitis (HR 1.058, 95% CI 1.015–1.103), with no significant differences in chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer [3]; this excess risk was most pronounced during the first 6 months of treatment (HR 1.143, 95% CI 1.055–1.239) [10], and was consistent in active-comparator analyses versus SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 1.054, 95% CI 1.014–1.096) [6]. Large-scale cardiovascular outcome trials and meta-analyses have not shown a statistically significant increase in acute pancreatitis compared to placebo, though pancreatitis remains a product-label warning and caution is advised in patients with a history of pancreatitis [8]. Mechanistically, GLP-1 RAs may raise lipase and amylase levels, impair gallbladder motility, and promote bile changes, plausibly contributing to early pancreatitis risk [4].

answer: In cardiovascular outcome and related trials, semaglutide has been associated with systolic blood pressure (SBP) reductions ranging from approximately 1.4 to 8.02 mmHg. A meta-analysis reported a significant SBP reduction of −8.02 mmHg with semaglutide, with a smaller diastolic reduction of −3.71 mmHg [3]. A broader analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonist cardiovascular outcome trials, including SUSTAIN-6, described SBP reductions of 1.4–5.4 mmHg [7]. In a real-world sub-analysis of the REALSEM-SP study, once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide reduced office SBP by −4 mmHg at 6 months and −2 mmHg at 12 months (p=0.014), with the greatest benefit in patients with uncontrolled baseline blood pressure [10]. A separate cohort treated with dapagliflozin plus semaglutide showed a mean SBP reduction from 137±17 to 131±17 mmHg (P=0.004) [2].

answer: Proposed weight-independent mechanisms by which GLP-1 receptor agonists lower blood pressure include improved endothelial function and reduced arterial stiffness [8], as well as natriuresis-mediated reduction in glomerular hyperfiltration and favorable hemodynamic effects [4]. Mechanistic analyses in non-diabetic obesity indicate that the observed 4.2 mmHg systolic blood pressure reduction exceeds what would be expected from weight loss alone (approximately 1 mmHg per kilogram), and the 39% reduction in hsCRP suggests direct anti-inflammatory and vascular-protective effects [5]. Additional proposed pathways include atherosclerotic plaque stabilization and reduction of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic signaling [2][7], and modulation of the renin-angiotensin system via enhanced MAS1-mediated signaling (the protective arm of the RAAS) and renin recruitment along the renal vasculature [6]. However, the precise mechanisms remain incompletely understood and causality cannot be definitively established [2][3].

answer: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce systolic blood pressure (SBP) by approximately 2–3 mmHg versus placebo through mechanisms including vasodilation, natriuresis, and decreased sympathetic activity [4], with meta-analytic data showing a more pronounced effect on SBP (−8.02 mmHg) than diastolic pressure (−3.71 mmHg) [2]. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 trials (145,322 participants), GLP-1RA significantly reduced MACE (pooled HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.81–0.91), and meta-regression showed that both SBP and weight reductions were independently associated with MACE risk reduction, with the BP–outcome relationship being stronger in trials using ambulatory BP monitoring [1]. These findings explicitly support the use of GLP-1RA in individuals with hypertension, including those with resistant phenotypes [1], and GLP-1RA (e.g., semaglutide) are recognized among additional therapeutic options offering antihypertensive and cardio-renal benefits in resistant hypertension, particularly in CKD [7]. However, the sources do not report dedicated trials or effect estimates of GLP-1RA specifically in treatment-refractory hypertension, and causality between BP control and cardiovascular outcomes cannot be definitively established [1].
